evidenceAudit.scope: Non-pregnant adults with type 2 diabetes in outpatient and primary care in Saudi Arabia. Content verified against SDCPG 2021 on 11 Oct 2026; clinical approval is pending.
findings: All targets, thresholds, intervals and doses in this version are taken from the cited SDCPG page.

SDCPG gives a metformin titration (500 mg once daily up to 1500–2000 mg daily) only in its prediabetes section; the type 2 diabetes treatment section names metformin first-line but restates no dose. Confirm the dose with the SFDA product information and the local formulary.
SDCPG 2021 predates newer international standards; drug-class recommendations (SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists) should be compared with current international standards before approval.

SFDA Saudi Drug Information System (searched 11 Oct 2026) lists metformin-containing products, insulin glargine, insulin aspart, insulin lispro, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, amlodipine, indapamide, spironolactone and statins. Registration does not confirm hospital formulary inclusion or stock.
unverifiedSections: Drug-specific doses for SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors and sulfonylureas (SDCPG gives class guidance only)
Figure-based content in SDCPG (glycaemic target factors, physical activity plan, statin flowcharts) that was not machine-readable
Pregnancy and children with type 2 diabetes (separate SDCPG sections)

pathophysiology.summary: Type 2 diabetes is a progressive loss of β-cell insulin secretion, frequently on a background of insulin resistance. Chronic hyperglycaemia, together with dyslipidaemia, hypertension and smoking, damages the arterial wall and drives atherosclerosis, which is why cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in diabetes. Sustained hyperglycaemia also causes microvascular damage to the retina, kidneys and nerves. In Saudi Arabia, risk is driven by family history, age, maternal diabetes or gestational diabetes, obesity, sedentary lifestyle and diet.
keyMechanisms: Insulin resistance plus progressive β-cell failure: explains why treatment usually needs to be intensified over time and why insulin may eventually be required.
Glucotoxicity: severe hyperglycaemia with catabolic features (weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia, ketosis) is why insulin is preferred when glucose is above 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L) or HbA1c above 10%.
Macrovascular disease: hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia, hypertension and smoking act together, so blood pressure, lipids and smoking are treatment targets alongside glucose.
Microvascular disease: the reason for scheduled eye, kidney and foot screening.
Saudi context: in the SPACE registry, 58.1% of patients with acute coronary syndrome had diabetes and presented about 10 years younger than in other countries.

symptoms: Often asymptomatic and found by screening: SDCPG recommends screening all adults from age 35, and earlier for overweight adults (BMI at least 25 kg/m² or abdominal obesity) with at least one risk factor.
Symptoms of hyperglycaemia: polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia and weight loss.

Symptoms of complications: blurred or changed vision, eye pain, numbness, burning or pain in the feet, claudication, erectile dysfunction, and symptoms of autonomic neuropathy (postural dizziness, gastroparesis, nocturnal diarrhoea).
Scope: non-pregnant adults. Pregnancy, gestational diabetes and children with type 2 diabetes follow separate SDCPG sections.
physicalSigns: Weight, BMI and waist circumference (abdominal obesity at least 102 cm in men and 88 cm in women).
Annual foot examination: gait, foot and toe shape, skin, nails, hygiene, pedal pulses, temperature and 10 g monofilament sensation.
Signs of insulin resistance such as acanthosis nigricans.
redFlags: Ketosis or ketoacidosis, or glucose at least 600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L) with drowsiness: same-day emergency assessment for DKA or HHS
Glucose above 300 mg/dL or HbA1c above 10% with weight loss or osmotic symptoms: start insulin without delay
Foot ulcer or signs of foot infection: immediate referral to the multidisciplinary foot team
Macular oedema, severe non-proliferative or any proliferative retinopathy: immediate referral to an ophthalmologist
eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²: stop metformin and refer to nephrology
New-onset diabetes in a lean adult without family history: consider pancreatic adenocarcinoma

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Absolute insulin deficiency, often with ketosis; may be suspected in younger or lean patients or when DKA is the presentation. Islet autoantibody testing and a specialist opinion help classify it.
Diabetes first diagnosed in the second or third trimester that was not overt before pregnancy; follows the pregnancy pathway.

differentials.condition: Monogenic diabetes (for example MODY or neonatal diabetes)
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Strong multigenerational family history and young onset without typical type 2 features; consider specialist genetic assessment.

differentials.condition: Diabetes from exocrine pancreatic disease (for example pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis or pancreatic cancer)
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: History of pancreatitis or malabsorption. New diabetes in a lean adult without a family history should raise suspicion of pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
Onset linked to glucocorticoids, atypical antipsychotics, antiretroviral therapy or anti-rejection drugs; review the medication list.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: At diagnosis; then twice a year if at target and stable, four times a year if above target or after a treatment change
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Diagnosis at 6.5% or above; prediabetes 5.7–6.4%. Usual target below 7%, individualised between 6.5% and 8%.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: The main measure of glycaemic control. If HbA1c is unreliable because of altered red-cell turnover or a haemoglobin variant, use fructosamine or total glycated haemoglobin.

ruleIn.testName: Fasting plasma glucose or 75 g OGTT
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Fasting glucose at least 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or 2-hour OGTT at least 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L); prediabetes fasting 100–125 mg/dL or 2-hour 140–199 mg/dL.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Without clear hyperglycaemic symptoms, diagnosis needs two abnormal results. A random glucose of 200 mg/dL or more is diagnostic only with classic symptoms or a hyperglycaemic crisis.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: At diagnosis and at least annually
ruleOut.expectedFinding: CKD if eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or ACR at least 2.0 mg/mmol on at least two of three samples over three months.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Albuminuria changes drug choice (ACE inhibitor or ARB; SGLT2 inhibitor if eGFR above 30). Active urinary sediment or rapid decline suggests another cause and needs nephrology.

ruleOut.testName: Comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist
ruleOut.modalityTarget: At diagnosis, then annually (more often with retinopathy)
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No retinopathy, or a graded retinopathy that sets the review interval.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Retinopathy is common in Saudi Arabia; macular oedema and severe or proliferative retinopathy need urgent treatment.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: At diagnosis; 2–3 months after starting or changing lipid-lowering therapy; then annually
ruleOut.expectedFinding: LDL, triglycerides and HDL relative to the treatment target.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Guides statin intensity. In adults aged 40 or over not on lipid-lowering therapy, repeat at least every five years.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: B12 periodically on long-term metformin; creatinine and potassium at baseline and at least annually on ACE inhibitor, ARB or diuretic
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Normal B12; stable creatinine and potassium.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Metformin can cause B12 deficiency and worsen neuropathy; ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics affect renal function and potassium.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the diagnosis and build the patient profile
actions: Confirm diagnosis with HbA1c, fasting glucose or OGTT (two abnormal results unless clearly symptomatic) and classify the diabetes type.
Complete the comprehensive evaluation: history, lifestyle, medicines, psychosocial factors, self-management skills, pregnancy plans, full examination and baseline laboratory tests.
Assess ASCVD risk (SDCPG suggests the ACC/AHA Risk Estimator Plus because there is no local calculator), heart failure, CKD stage and hypoglycaemia risk; repeat at least annually.
Screen for depression at diagnosis and annually.

branches.condition: Ketosis, glucose at least 600 mg/dL or reduced consciousness
actions: Refer the same day to the emergency department for DKA or HHS assessment.

branches.condition: Glucose above 300 mg/dL or HbA1c above 10%, or catabolic symptoms
actions: Start insulin (or a GLP-1 receptor agonist) now rather than waiting for oral therapy to fail.

clinicalManagement.title: Agree individual targets with the patient
clinicalManagement.timeframe: First visit and reviewed at every visit
actions: HbA1c target below 7% for most adults; individualise between 6.5% and 8% depending on hypoglycaemia risk, comorbidity and patient priorities.
Blood pressure: below 130/80 mmHg if 10-year ASCVD risk is above 15%; below 140/90 mmHg if risk is below 15%, if achievable safely.
Lipids: statin intensity according to age, ASCVD and risk (moderate intensity for primary prevention aged 40–75; high intensity for established ASCVD).

clinicalManagement.title: Start lifestyle treatment and structured education
clinicalManagement.timeframe: From diagnosis, reinforced at each visit
actions: Refer to structured diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES).
Individual nutrition plan from a registered nutritionist; aim for more than 5% weight loss if overweight; avoid sugar-sweetened drinks; sodium limit 2,300 mg/day.
Individualised physical activity after pre-exercise assessment; advise about 7 hours of sleep; smoking cessation counselling at every visit.

clinicalManagement.title: Start and intensify glucose-lowering treatment
actions: Metformin is first line unless contraindicated (eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²).
If HbA1c is more than 1.5% above target at diagnosis, start dual therapy.
If the target is not met after about three months, add a second agent chosen by patient factors: sulfonylurea, pioglitazone, DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT2 inhibitor, GLP-1 receptor agonist or basal insulin.
Do not delay intensification when targets are not met.
Add an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit.

branches.condition: Heart failure, or ASCVD at high risk of heart failure
actions: Use an SGLT2 inhibitor.

branches.condition: CKD with eGFR above 30 and albuminuria
actions: Use an SGLT2 inhibitor; if not tolerated, or if eGFR is below 30, add a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit.

branches.condition: Insulin needed (HbA1c above 10%, glucose consistently above 300 mg/dL, catabolic symptoms, or above target on three or more agents for at least three months)
actions: Start basal insulin 0.1–0.2 units/kg/day if HbA1c is below 8%, or 0.2–0.3 units/kg/day if HbA1c is above 8%; titrate by 2 units every third day to the fasting target.
Add prandial insulin (4–5 units or 10% of the basal dose with the largest meal) if post-meal glucose stays high; titrate by 1–2 units or 10% every 2–3 days.
Review every two weeks until self-monitored glucose is near target.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat blood pressure, lipids and antiplatelet needs
clinicalManagement.timeframe: From diagnosis; review at least annually
actions: Use drug classes that reduce cardiovascular events: ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide-like diuretic or dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.
ACE inhibitor or ARB first line when urine ACR is 30 mg/g or more.
Statin by intensity (moderate: atorvastatin 10–20 mg or rosuvastatin 5–10 mg; high: atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg).
Aspirin for secondary prevention; individualise for primary prevention in high-risk patients; clopidogrel 75 mg if aspirin is not tolerated.
Start two drugs or a single-pill combination with lifestyle treatment.

branches.condition: Blood pressure uncontrolled on three classes including a diuretic
actions: Add a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.

clinicalManagement.title: Screen for complications and refer early
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis, then at least annually
actions: Eye examination by an ophthalmologist; urine ACR and eGFR; foot examination with 10 g monofilament and 128 Hz tuning fork; neuropathy assessment.
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast) in CKD; protein intake 0.8 g/kg/day for non-dialysis CKD.

branches.condition: Any macular oedema, severe non-proliferative or proliferative retinopathy
actions: Refer immediately to an experienced ophthalmologist.
Treat urgently through a multidisciplinary foot team; offload and debride as indicated.

branches.condition: eGFR below 30, uncertain cause of CKD, rapid decline or BP not at target
actions: Refer to nephrology.
Arrange ankle–brachial index and specialist referral.

medicationPlan.note: Non-pregnant adults. Doses are as stated in SDCPG 2021 at the cited page. SDCPG gives class-level guidance for SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors and sulfonylureas without drug doses; take those from the SFDA product information and local formulary. SFDA registration checked 11 Oct 2026.

regimens.patientGroup: Adults with type 2 diabetes and eGFR above 30 mL/min/1.73 m²
regimens.dose: Start 500 mg once daily and increase as tolerated to 1500–2000 mg daily (titration stated in the SDCPG prediabetes section; the T2DM section restates no dose)
regimens.frequency: Once or twice daily depending on formulation
regimens.duration: Long term unless not tolerated or contraindicated
adjustments: Contraindicated if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²
Withhold on the day of radiocontrast and restart after 1–2 days once renal function is confirmed
monitoring: Periodic vitamin B12, especially with anaemia or neuropathy

regimens.patientGroup: Adults with HbA1c above 10%, glucose consistently above 300 mg/dL, catabolic symptoms, or above target on three or more agents
regimens.dose: 0.1–0.2 units/kg/day if HbA1c is below 8%; 0.2–0.3 units/kg/day if HbA1c is above 8%
regimens.duration: Long term; reassess as control improves
adjustments: Titrate by 2 units every third day to the fasting glucose target
monitoring: Review every two weeks until near target

regimens.indication: Prandial insulin when post-meal glucose stays high on basal insulin
regimens.patientGroup: Adults on basal insulin with fasting glucose at or near target but HbA1c above target
regimens.genericName: Rapid-acting prandial insulin (for example insulin aspart)
regimens.dose: 4–5 units or 10% of the basal dose with the largest meal
regimens.frequency: With the largest meal; add other meals as needed
adjustments: Titrate by 1–2 units or 10% every 2–3 days to the 2-hour post-meal target

regimens.indication: Lipid lowering, moderate intensity (primary prevention, age 40–75 without ASCVD)
adjustments: Use high intensity (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg) for established ASCVD or multiple risk factors
monitoring: Lipid profile 2–3 months after starting or changing dose, then annually

regimens.indication: Antiplatelet therapy for secondary prevention when aspirin is not tolerated
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with diabetes and established ASCVD
adjustments: Aspirin is first choice for secondary prevention; SDCPG gives no aspirin dose

teaching.scope: Non-pregnant adults with type 2 diabetes in outpatient and primary care. Pregnancy, gestational diabetes, children and in-hospital hyperglycaemia are covered elsewhere.
learningObjectives: Explain how insulin resistance and progressive β-cell failure lead to rising glucose and to macro- and microvascular complications.
Diagnose type 2 diabetes correctly, including when one abnormal result is enough.
Set individual HbA1c, blood pressure and lipid targets with the patient.
Choose and intensify glucose-lowering treatment according to ASCVD, heart failure, CKD and hypoglycaemia risk.
Run an annual review that screens eyes, kidneys, feet, mood and cardiovascular risk.

vignette.text: Fictitious teaching case. A 48-year-old woman in Riyadh has an HbA1c of 8.9% on a workplace screen and a repeat fasting glucose of 9.4 mmol/L. She has no symptoms. She had gestational diabetes 12 years ago, her BMI is 33 kg/m², her blood pressure is 146/92 mmHg and she has a previous myocardial infarction. eGFR is 72 mL/min/1.73 m² and urine ACR 45 mg/g. Ramadan starts in four months.

guidedApproach.title: Step 1 · Confirm and classify
guidedApproach.guidance: Yes. Two abnormal results (HbA1c at least 6.5% and fasting glucose at least 7.0 mmol/L) in an asymptomatic person. Her history and BMI fit type 2 diabetes.

guidedApproach.title: Step 2 · Profile her risk
guidedApproach.prompt: Which comorbidities change your drug choices?
guidedApproach.guidance: Established ASCVD (previous MI) and albuminuria (ACR 30 mg/g or more) with eGFR above 30.

guidedApproach.title: Step 3 · Agree targets
guidedApproach.guidance: HbA1c below 7% if achievable safely. With ASCVD her cardiovascular risk is high, so aim for blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg. High-intensity statin for secondary prevention.

guidedApproach.title: Step 4 · Start treatment
guidedApproach.prompt: HbA1c is 1.9% above a 7% target. One drug or two?
guidedApproach.guidance: More than 1.5% above target, so start dual therapy: metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit, because of her MI and albuminuria.

guidedApproach.title: Step 5 · Blood pressure and kidneys
guidedApproach.guidance: An ACE inhibitor or ARB, because ACR is 30 mg/g or more. Check creatinine and potassium at baseline and after starting.

guidedApproach.title: Step 6 · Annual screening
guidedApproach.prompt: What else must happen this year?
guidedApproach.guidance: Ophthalmology eye examination, foot examination with monofilament, lipid profile, depression screen, structured education and nutrition referral.

guidedApproach.title: Step 7 · Ramadan
guidedApproach.guidance: Assess her risk category before Ramadan. Her ASCVD may place her in a higher-risk group; agree a plan, adjust timings, and teach her to break the fast if glucose is below 3.9 mmol/L or above 16.7 mmol/L.

checkpoints.question: An asymptomatic patient has one HbA1c of 6.8%. Can you diagnose diabetes?
checkpoints.answer: Not yet. Without clear hyperglycaemic symptoms SDCPG requires two abnormal results, either the same test repeated or two different tests.

checkpoints.question: When should you start two glucose-lowering drugs at diagnosis?
checkpoints.answer: When HbA1c is more than 1.5% above the individual target.

checkpoints.question: Which patients should be offered an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist regardless of HbA1c?
checkpoints.answer: Those with established ASCVD (either class with proven benefit), heart failure or high heart-failure risk (SGLT2 inhibitor), and CKD with albuminuria and eGFR above 30 (SGLT2 inhibitor, or a GLP-1 receptor agonist if not tolerated or eGFR is below 30).

checkpoints.question: When should metformin be stopped?
checkpoints.answer: When eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², if not tolerated, and temporarily on the day of radiocontrast until renal function is confirmed 1–2 days later.

checkpoints.question: What should a patient do if glucose is 17.5 mmol/L while fasting in Ramadan?
checkpoints.answer: Break the fast. SDCPG advises breaking the fast if glucose is below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or above 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L).

pitfalls: Diagnosing on a single abnormal result in an asymptomatic patient.
Delaying insulin when HbA1c is above 10% or the patient is losing weight.
Choosing a second drug only on cost when the patient has ASCVD, heart failure or CKD.
Using HbA1c alone when anaemia or a haemoglobin variant makes it unreliable.
Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.
Forgetting B12 on long-term metformin, or kidney and potassium checks on ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics.
Letting a patient fast in Ramadan without a pre-Ramadan risk assessment and dose plan.
keyPoints: Screen all Saudi adults from age 35, and earlier if overweight with a risk factor.
HbA1c below 7% for most adults, individualised from 6.5% to 8%.
Metformin first; intensify every 3–6 months; do not delay.
Comorbidity drives drug choice: ASCVD, heart failure and CKD point to SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Every year: eyes, kidneys (ACR and eGFR), feet, lipids, mood and cardiovascular risk.
Plan for Ramadan before it starts.

references.title: Saudi Diabetes Clinical Practice Guidelines (SDCPG)
references.edition: First edition 2021, Saudi National Diabetes Center / Saudi Health Council (no newer edition located on 11 Oct 2026)

references.title: SFDA Saudi Drug Information System (registration search)

patientEducation: Structured self-management education at diagnosis, annually, when complications develop and at transitions of care.
Self-monitoring of glucose for people on insulin, including before driving and exercise and when hypoglycaemia is suspected.
Foot self-care and appropriate footwear for those at high risk.
Ramadan: pre-Ramadan risk assessment, dose and timing changes for sulfonylureas and insulin, self-monitoring, and breaking the fast below 3.9 mmol/L or above 16.7 mmol/L.
lifestyleAndDiet: Individual nutrition plan from a registered nutritionist; Mediterranean-style eating pattern; avoid sugar-sweetened drinks.
Weight loss of more than 5% if overweight or obese.
Individualised physical activity after pre-exercise assessment; about 7 hours of sleep; stop smoking.
mdtReferrals: Ophthalmology for screening and for retinopathy needing treatment.
Multidisciplinary foot team for high-risk feet, ulcers or infection.
Nephrology for eGFR below 30, unclear cause, rapid decline or uncontrolled BP.
Mental health provider when screening is positive or distress affects self-care.
dischargeCriteria: Not applicable as an inpatient discharge; continuing care is in primary care or the diabetes clinic.
Patient understands targets, medicines, monitoring and when to seek urgent help.
Next review date, laboratory tests and referrals are booked with a named clinician.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review every 3–6 months to reassess HbA1c and adjust treatment (every 3 months if above target or after a change; every 6 months if stable at target). Hold a full annual review covering eyes, kidneys, feet, lipids, cardiovascular risk and mood. Review every two weeks after starting insulin until glucose is near target.

Investigations.title: Annual review
Investigations.timeframe: At diagnosis and at least yearly

steps.clinical_question: Is the individual glycaemic target met?
steps.decision_rationale: If above target for about three months, intensify treatment.

steps.clinical_question: Is there kidney disease that changes drug choice?
steps.expected_finding: ACR below 30 mg/g and eGFR at least 60
steps.decision_rationale: Albuminuria leads to an ACE inhibitor or ARB and an SGLT2 inhibitor; eGFR below 30 stops metformin and triggers nephrology referral.

steps.clinical_question: Is there retinopathy or macular oedema?
steps.decision_rationale: Any macular oedema or severe or proliferative retinopathy needs immediate referral.

steps.test: Foot examination with 10 g monofilament and 128 Hz tuning fork
steps.clinical_question: Is the foot at risk of ulceration?
steps.decision_rationale: At-risk feet need education, footwear and closer review; claudication or absent pulses need ABI.
steps.timeframe: Annually, more often if high risk

steps.clinical_question: Is LDL at target on the right statin intensity?
steps.decision_rationale: Adjust statin intensity; recheck 2–3 months after a change.

actions.instruction: Dual therapy at diagnosis if HbA1c is more than 1.5% above target.
Add a second or third agent chosen by comorbidity and patient factors if not at target.
Basal insulin 0.1–0.3 units/kg/day (by HbA1c) titrated by 2 units every third day; add prandial insulin if needed.

loading_dose.reason: No loading dose; start at a weight-based daily dose and titrate.

maintenance_dose.duration: Titrate by 2 units every third day to the fasting target

contraindications: Hypoglycaemia at the time of dosing
adjustments: Lower starting range (0.1–0.2 units/kg/day) if HbA1c is below 8%
monitoring: Review every two weeks until near target
